meta.title: Who really said "Legal Advice: Pound the Facts, Pound the Law, Pound the Table"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Alan Dershowitz. Quote Investigator calls this courtroom adage anonymous; the earliest known version is a footnote in an 1911 advocacy treatise.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Legal Advice: Pound the Facts, Pound the Law, Pound the Table'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to 1911 and calls it anonymous. Dershowitz, Holmes, Michael and Sandburg have all been credited; none is its documented author.

answer.label: Not Alan Dershowitz — an anonymous lawyers' adage
answer.authorDates: Documented in print from 1911 · originator unidentified
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traced this courtroom saying back to 1911 and concluded that it “evolved over time,” recommending an anonymous attribution. The earliest documented version is a footnote in Byron K. and William F. Elliott’s advocacy treatise The Work of the Advocate — and even there the punch line is credited only to an unnamed “modern commentator.” Dershowitz is one of several later names the adage was pinned on.

source.heading: The earliest documented version

docMeta.dd: The Work of the Advocate: A Practical Treatise, 2nd ed.
Byron K. Elliott and William F. Elliott · Bobbs-Merrill, Indianapolis, 1911 · page 390, footnote 17
Three-fold “hammer” version by 1934; Carl Sandburg’s The People, Yes in 1936; the modern “pound” triad in print by 1956

source.excerpt: “If you have a case where the law is clearly on your side, but the facts and justice seem to be against you,” said an old lawyer to his son, who was about to begin the practice of the law, “urge upon the jury the vast importance of sustaining the law. On the other hand, if the law is against you, or doubtful, and the facts show that your case is founded in justice, insist that justice be done though the heavens fall.” “But,” said the young man, “how shall I manage a case where both the law and the facts are dead against me?” “In that case,” replied the old lawyer, “talk around it,” and “the worse it is, the harder you pound the table,” adds a modern commentator.
trail: 1911 — the earliest version located by Quote Investigator ↗ appears in a footnote of the Elliotts’ The Work of the Advocate ↗, in a long-winded form ending “the worse it is, the harder you pound the table.”
1915 – 1925 — retellings in A History of Northwest Missouri and The Rotarian keep the structure but end by abusing the opposing attorney rather than the furniture, as QI documents ↗.
1934 – 1936 — the first three-fold repetition QI finds runs in Golden Book Magazine, and Carl Sandburg folds a version into The People, Yes, which QI credits ↗ with popularising it.

1956 → 2007 — the adage acquires owners: Holmes in a 1956 newspaper column, Jerome Michael in a 1985 Parade recollection, Alan Dershowitz in a 2007 column — all catalogued, and none substantiated, by Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: From the footnote at the foot of page 390 of the 1911 second edition — confirmed in the Internet Archive scan ↗. Note that the Elliotts do not claim the line: the table-pounding half is quoted from an unnamed “modern commentator.” The tidy three-part wording people quote today is not here yet.

sourceLink.text: The Work of the Advocate (1911) at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Two separate answers here. The 1911 Elliott text quoted above was published in the United States well before 1931 and is public domain — the Internet Archive’s copy is marked not in copyright. But the popular modern wording on this page is a different string: an anonymous adage whose first appearance has never been pinned to an identified author or publication, so no rights status is asserted for it. Carl Sandburg’s 1936 rendering in The People, Yes is its own case and is not the wording quoted here.

author.name: Byron Kosciusko Elliott
author.heading: The judge who wrote it down first
author.metaLine: 1835–1913 · Indiana Supreme Court justice and legal-treatise author
author.bio: Byron K. Elliott was an Indianapolis lawyer who served as city attorney, sat on the Marion County criminal and superior courts, and was a justice of the Indiana Supreme Court from 1881 to 1893. After leaving the bench he practised with his son, William F. Elliott, and the two wrote a shelf of legal treatises that were used across the United States. He did not coin this saying. His 1911 treatise simply records it — and his own footnote hands the famous table-pounding line to an anonymous “modern commentator,” which is why the adage remains, as Quote Investigator puts it, anonymous.

misattribution.heading: Four names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This is a saying that attracts owners. Quote Investigator ↗ opens its investigation by listing five candidates and Anonymous — and lands on Anonymous.

items.why: The version pinned on Dershowitz is the one Quote Investigator set out to check: a 2007 newspaper column describing the Harvard Law professor telling students to pound the facts, the law, or the table. But the saying was already in print in 1911, and QI’s verdict is anonymous rather than Dershowitz — see the investigation ↗. It is also absent from Wikiquote’s page for him ↗.

A 1956 Los Angeles Times column quoted the “pound the law / pound the facts / pound the table” triad as an admonition of Holmes. Quote Investigator ↗ reports finding no compelling evidence supporting the claim.

In a 1985 Parade article the literary agent Morton L. Janklow recalled Michael delivering the “hammer” version as his final words on advocacy. Quote Investigator ↗ accepts that Michael used it in teaching but notes he graduated from Columbia Law School in 1912 — after the adage was already in print — so he probably did not craft it.

Sandburg put a version in his 1936 book-length poem The People, Yes, a work built out of sayings then circulating in America. Quote Investigator ↗ credits him with helping to popularize the expression, not with originating it — and his wording ends with pounding the table and yelling like hell, not with the neat modern triad.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: the saying evolved over time and should carry an anonymous attribution. Its earliest documented appearance is a footnote in a 1911 treatise whose authors themselves credited the line to an unnamed “modern commentator.”

context.heading: Why the table gets pounded
lead: The line survives because it is a joke with a real theory of advocacy inside it. Every version says the same thing: an argument has ranked resources — the evidence, the governing law, and, when both fail, sheer performance. It is the bar’s own wry admission that a courtroom is a room with an audience in it.

That is also why nobody can own it. The versions Quote Investigator collects are folk retellings rather than a text being copied: a father advising a son, an old lawyer advising a young one, a professor’s parting words in the last minute of the last class. Each teller polishes it. By the time it reaches a Harvard classroom in the 2000s it has been sharpened for eighty years, and the sharpening — not the invention — is what people remember.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording tightened, decade by decade
detailsBody: The 1911 footnote is wordy: a long exchange about sustaining the law, justice being done though the heavens fall, and only then the table. The comic three-part structure is not yet there.

By 1934, Quote Investigator ↗ finds the first three-fold repetition — using “hammer,” and ending not with the table but with hammering opposing counsel, the same punch line as the 1915 and 1925 tellings.
The “pound” triad that people quote today is on the page by 1956, in a Los Angeles Times column that credits it — without support — to Oliver Wendell Holmes.
context.pull: “The worse it is, the harder you pound the table.”

schema.quotationText: When the facts are on your side, pound the facts. When the law is on your side, pound the law. When neither is on your side, pound the table.
schema.alternateName: If you have the facts on your side, hammer the facts. If you have the law on your side, hammer the law. If you have neither the facts nor the law, hammer the table.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this saying, traced it back to 1911, and concluded it evolved over time and should carry an anonymous attribution; it lists Carl Sandburg, Alan Dershowitz, Jerome Michael, Jacob J. Rosenblum, Oliver Wendell Holmes and Anonymous as candidates.

QI's earliest citation is the 1911 second edition of The Work of the Advocate by Byron K. Elliott and William F. Elliott (Bobbs-Merrill, Indianapolis), footnote 17, page 390, ending 'the worse it is, the harder you pound the table,' adds a modern commentator.
QI records a 1956 Los Angeles Times column attributing the pound-the-table triad to Oliver Wendell Holmes and states it found no compelling supporting evidence for that claim.

QI records Morton L. Janklow's 1985 Parade article crediting his Columbia teacher Jerome Michael with the 'hammer the facts / hammer the law / hammer the table' version, and notes Michael graduated from Columbia Law School in 1912 so probably did not craft the aphorism.

QI records Carl Sandburg's 1936 The People, Yes version ('if the law and the evidence are both against you, then pound on the table and yell like hell') and credits Sandburg with helping to popularize the expression.

The Dershowitz attribution QI is investigating comes from a modern column describing the Harvard Law professor telling students to pound the facts, the law, or the table; Dershowitz is not QI's conclusion.

QI records a 1934 Golden Book Magazine item (Jacob J. Rosenblum) as its earliest three-fold 'hammer' version, ending with hammering opposing counsel, and 1915/1925 retellings that end by abusing the opposing attorney.

The 1911 second edition of The Work of the Advocate contains the passage verbatim: 'If you have a case where the law is clearly on your side... talk around it,' and 'the worse it is, the harder you pound the table,' adds a modern commentator — complete in the footnote at the foot of page 390 (the running head 'ADDRESS TO JURY. 391' follows it; only the body text continues onto 391). The word 'hammer' does not appear in the footnote.

The Internet Archive item is The Work of the Advocate by Byron K. Elliott (1835-1913) and William F. Elliott (b. 1859), published 1911 by The Bobbs-Merrill Company, Indianapolis, with a full searchable text scan, and is marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

Byron Kosciusko Elliott (September 4, 1835 – April 19, 1913) was an American lawyer, judge and jurist from Indiana who served as Indianapolis city attorney, judge of the Marion County criminal and superior courts, and a justice of the Indiana Supreme Court from 1881 to 1893, and co-authored legal treatises with his son William F. Elliott.

Garson O'Toole's 3 July 2010 ADS-L post (message 100611, 18:16:55 UTC) presents the 1911 Elliott & Elliott citation (2nd edition, footnote 17, page 390, Bobbs-Merrill, Indianapolis) and notes the 1894 edition apparently lacked the footnote.
Wikiquote's Alan Dershowitz page does not contain the 'pound the facts / pound the law / pound the table' or 'hammer the facts' saying in any section.
Quote Investigator's Alan Dershowitz category page lists the 'Legal Advice: Pound the Facts, Pound the Law, Pound the Table' investigation under his name.
